4.3 - Layout Detection
After realizing that using OCR directly on the entire newspaper page wasn’t a viable option, due to the resolution of pages I got, I understood that a layout detection step needed to be integrated into the pipeline.
This stage would allow me to identify every article block present on each page. By isolating these regions, I could extract and process them individually using the VLM-based OCR engine without exceeding VRAM limits. The layout detection also provided some additional structural information that would later be used during article segmentation.
At first, I explored layout detection models available on platforms like Hugging Face, hoping to find an easy solution to implement and adapt to my needs. However, most of these models were trained on high quality modern documents, which did not match the degraded, multicolumn nature of historical newspapers. Given the complexity of the task of handling multicolumn layouts across a century of newspaper pages, with significant variation between each decade in formatting. I decided to focus on SOTA (state of the art) layout detection models capable of working with complex document structures like newspapers.
I then selected a fine-tuned model, his name is YOLO11-Document-Layout-Analysis, based on the YOLO11 (You only look once) architecture, but it has been adapted using a dataset well known in document layout recognition named DocLayNet. The model was first made for object recognition.

This model worked reasonably well, however to avoid losing too many articles blocks, it was necessary to lower the confidence threshold for the bounding boxes detection. To improve the quality of the layout detection, I implemented a set of custom rules aimed at reducing false positives and merging related text blocks into coherent zones. The idea came from a presentation I attended during the first week of my internship, where researchers specializing in historical document analysis discussed combining machine learning with rule-based post-processing to enhance detection accuracy.
Inspired by this approach, I developed a series of logic-based rules focused on the position and size of each bounding box, the proximity between neighboring boxes and their potential collisions or overlaps, which could indicate that they belong to the same article.

4.3.1 - The Ensemble Approach
After realizing that a single layout detection model even with rule-based post-processing was not sufficient to handle the entire diversity of newspaper pages from 1899 to the 1990s, I began exploring alternative strategies that I already knew from prior work. One approach commonly used in the data science field, and well suited to this kind of challenge.
The principle behind ensembling is simple yet powerful, by combining multiple models with different strengths and weaknesses. We can compensate for individual fragility while leveraging each models unique advantages. This leads to more robust and accurate predictions than what any single model could achieve on its own.
To implement this, I needed a second model that could provide high confidence predictions on layout detection, particularly in complex or degraded areas where the first model struggled. This led me to explore additional tools and ultimately build a hybrid system that combined both models outputs in an effective way.
This led me to adopt PP-DocLayout-L, a document layout detection model developed by PaddleOCR, released on March 21, 2025. It’s the largest version of the model, specifically designed for complex document structures and high-resolution images.
Unlike the YOLO based model I had previously tested which was fast but produced many overlapping or redundant bounding boxes, PP-DocLayout-L generated fewer boxes but more confident detections, especially in dense or damaged regions. However, the model occasionally misses smaller or less structured blocks.
To make the most of both models, I implemented a hybrid system that works as follows : 
Since PP-DocLayout-L tends to produce high-confidence predictions, I decided to treat its output as the primary layout detection source. In other words, when it detects a block, I consider it to be more likely accurate compared to the YOLO-based model.
Therefore, the process begins by applying the bounding boxes detected by PP-DocLayout-L. These provide a clean and reliable base structure for most pages, especially those that are degraded or have extremely complex layouts.
Next, I used the output from the YOLO-based model, but this time without applying the stricter filtering rules that were previously used to reduce noise. Instead, these less-filtered results were used to fill gaps where PP-DocLayout-L missed the little zone of the document.
The idea was simple, we start by using the most reliable detections from PP-DocLayout-L, then we use YOLO to find extra blocks that might have been missed. Finally we combine both sets of results and clean them up with some final merging rules that allow us to extend some of the original boxes. This way, I could get the best of both models. The final stage of the indexing pipeline is article segmentation, which aims to group the previously detected text blocks into full articles. This task proved to be one of the most complex parts of the pipeline due to the diversity of newspaper layouts, varying content types and the lack of clear semantic or structural patterns across decades.
At the time of writing, article segmentation remained under exploration, and no fully reliable solution had been finalized. However, I tested several promising strategies that can serve as a foundation for future development
4.4.1 - Embedding-Based Clustering
My first approach involved using semantic embeddings to represent each text block as a vector capturing its meaning. Using these vectors, I built a similarity matrix to identify blocks with related content, hoping to use clustering algorithms to group them accordingly.

As we see in the Similarity matrix, there are too few instances of high similarity between the sentences. I then applied HDBSCAN, a density-based clustering algorithm, to automatically detect clusters of semantically similar blocks. However, results were inconsistent :
* Many blocks contained short or fragmented text, making it difficult to extract meaningful themes.
* There was little correlation between neighboring blocks based on semantics alone.
* The model struggled to differentiate articles in the page, and wasn’t able to order blocks that composed articles
This experiment showed that purely semantic approaches are not sufficient for this task without additional contextual or spatial information.
4.4.2 - LLM-Based Grouping Strategy
Given the limitations of the embedding-based method, I explored an alternative using Large Language Models (LLMs). The idea was to pass both the text content and bounding box coordinates of each block to the LLM, asking it to predict which blocks should be grouped together.

* Input size became too large when combining many blocks, leading to higher GPU requirements.
* Spatial relationships were not clearly interpreted by the model, even after normalizing coordinate values.
